title: Grandma in Polish: Babcia, Busia and Every Family Word
excerpt: Grandma in Polish is babcia. Learn to say it, decline it, and where Polish-American family words like busia, busha and dziadziu come from.
metaDescription: Grandma in Polish is babcia. Learn to say it, decline it, and where Polish-American family words like busia, busha and dziadziu come from.
tags: polish words for grandma and grandpa
summary: The standard word for grandma in Polish is babcia (BAHP-chah), and you say babciu when you speak directly to her.
Grandpa is dziadek, with affectionate forms dziadzio and dziadziuś; grandparents together are dziadkowie.
Busia, busha and babci are Polish-American family words; busia is most likely a child's clipping of babusia, though no dictionary documents it.
Poland celebrates Dzień Babci on 21 January and Dzień Dziadka on 22 January.

factNotes: Origin of busia/busha is NOT documented in any dictionary I could find (sjp.pl only lists 'busia' as a form of 'buś' = young bull). The article presents 'clipped from babusia' explicitly as the most plausible explanation, not fact; the BOO-shah = busha spelling point is just Polish orthography. The transparent.com blog (busha/busia/babusza 'not correct Polish', many US families say babci/babciu) timed out on direct fetch; its content was read only via search-result excerpts, so the article attributes it loosely ('a Polish-language learning blog'). 'Jaja' as a grandpa word could not be sourced; only 'Jaju' = dziadziu is sourced (Harvard Magazine). Gigi: no authoritative origin found; article only says it is a general American nickname, not Polish. The 'babci from do babci' and 'baba from other Slavic languages entering immigrant families' explanations are hedged as likely, not stated as fact. Dzień Dziadka origin ('probably brought from America in the 1980s') is hedged as Polish Wikipedia's wording. Note for coordinator: the live /blog/family-members-in-polish intro claims 'Polish has distinct words for maternal and paternal grandparents', which is wrong; this article (correctly) says babcia/dziadek cover both sides.
